ext.title: Breaking the Sorting Barrier for Directed SSSP
ext.venue: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2504.17033v2 [cs.DS] (v2 stamped 30 Jul 2025; title page dated July 31, 2025). The text does not state a venue. The later STOC 2025 listing in Paul's bib docx cannot be verified from this file.
ext.document_type: Theoretical computer science preprint (algorithm design and worst-case analysis)
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 960 lines of _text/203c3d9d4ab6.txt (51,509 chars), in chunks, through the references (pp. 1-17). All 26 annotation items in _annots/203c3d9d4ab6.json were read; the file contains one JSON array only. Metadata hint was correct on title and authors (author order matches). Year 2025 confirmed. ext.research_question: Can single-source shortest paths (SSSP) on directed graphs with real non-negative edge weights be solved faster than Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) bound on sparse graphs, in the comparison-addition model, and can the Omega(n log n) sorting barrier be broken for this problem?
ext.theory: Dijkstra's algorithm sorts vertices by distance through a priority queue, which costs Theta(n log n) on the frontier. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges in k rounds with no sorting. The paper merges the two ideas through recursive partitioning, in the style of bottleneck-path algorithms (Gabow-Tarjan 1988; Chechik et al. 2016; Duan et al. 2018), so that the frontier is shrunk to pivots before any sorting (pp. 2-4). The sorting cost is reduced by a block-based partial-sorting structure (Lemma 3.3, pp. 6-7). The paper does not present a behavioural or social theory.
ext.data: No empirical data. The analysis is over worst-case inputs: directed graph G=(V,E) with n vertices, m edges, and non-negative real weights w: E to R>=0. The algorithm first transforms G into a constant-degree graph G' with O(m) vertices and O(m) edges via zero-weight cycles (Sec. 2, p. 3). The bound assumes m = O(n) (p. 4). No sample, N, or time period applies.
ext.method: Deterministic algorithm design plus worst-case running-time analysis. The core procedure is a recursive bounded multi-source shortest path routine, BMSSP(l, B, S) (Algorithm 3, p. 10). It uses FindPivots (Algorithm 1, p. 6), a base case that is a mini-Dijkstra (Algorithm 2, p. 9), and a partial-sort block-list data structure D (Lemma 3.3, pp. 6-8). Parameters are k = floor(log^(1/3) n) and t = floor(log^(2/3) n), with recursion depth ceil(log n / t) (Sec. 3.1, p. 4). Correctness is proved by induction on level l (Lemma 3.7, pp. 12-13). Time is bounded in Lemma 3.12 (p. 14).
ext.identification: Not applicable. This is a worst-case complexity result, not a statistical or causal identification strategy.
ext.scope: Population: directed graphs with real non-negative weights, sparse regime m = O(n) after a constant-degree transformation. Model: comparison-addition only (each addition and comparison takes unit time; no other operations on weights). Era: 2025 arXiv preprint. Institutions: Tsinghua University, Stanford University, and Max Planck Institute for Informatics (author affiliations, p. 2 footnotes). The paper does not address lobbying, networks as social objects, elections, persuasion, turnout, legislators, or text measurement.

key_findings.finding: Main result: a deterministic SSSP algorithm for directed graphs with real non-negative weights in time O(m log^(2/3) n), the first to break the O(m + n log n) bound of Dijkstra on sparse graphs.

The result is also the first deterministic algorithm to beat O(m + n log n) for SSSP even on undirected graphs, since the prior O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) SSSP algorithm of Duan, Mao, Shu, Yin (DMSY23) is randomized.
key_findings.location: Sec. 1, p. 2 (remark after Theorem 1.1); DMSY23 cited on p. 1
key_findings.numbers: DMSY23: O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) randomized, undirected

key_findings.finding: Dijkstra is optimal if the output must include the vertex ordering by distance (Haeupler et al. 2024), so the improvement applies to distances without a full ordering.
key_findings.location: Sec. 1, p. 1 (citing HHR+24); Sec. 3.1 p. 4 ('without necessarily recovering a complete ordering')

key_findings.finding: Key idea: shrink the frontier. For a bound B, the frontier S is reduced to pivots of size at most |eU|/k, where k = log^(Omega(1)) n. Each pivot roots a shortest-path tree of at least k vertices.
key_findings.location: Technical overview, Sec. 1.1, p. 2; FindPivots Lemma 3.2, p. 5

key_findings.finding: Per-vertex running time is reduced from Theta(log n) to log n / log^(Omega(1)) n through divide-and-conquer over log n / t levels.
Parameter choice that yields the final bound: k = floor(log^(1/3) n), t = floor(log^(2/3) n), recursion level l = ceil(log n / t).
key_findings.location: Sec. 3.1, p. 4; Lemma 3.12 final statement, p. 14
key_findings.numbers: k = floor(log^(1/3) n); t = floor(log^(2/3) n); l = ceil(log n / t)

key_findings.finding: Output-size bound for each BMSSP call: the returned set U has size at most 4k^(2lt), and a partial run has |U| at least k^(2lt).
Running-time bound for a BMSSP call at level l.
key_findings.numbers: C(k + 2t/k)(l+1)|U| + C(t + l log k)|N+_[min S d(x), B)(U)|

key_findings.finding: Total running time over recursion depth: depth is O(log^(1/3) n) and FindPivots costs O(nk) per depth, so the sum is O(nk (log n)/t) = O(n log^(2/3) n). Batch-prepend overhead is O(n log^(1/3) n log log n).
key_findings.numbers: depth O(log^(1/3) n); per-depth cost O(nk); overall O(n log^(2/3) n); batch-prepend O(n log^(1/3) n log log n)

key_findings.finding: Structure of recursion: children's output sets U_y are disjoint, and the sum of |U_x| over all nodes of the recursion tree is O(n log n / t).
Data structure D (partial sorting with block lists) supports insert in amortized O(max{1, log(N/M)}), batch prepend in O(L max{1, log(L/M)}), and pull in O(|S'|).
key_findings.numbers: insert O(max{1, log(N/M)}); batch prepend O(L max{1, log(L/M)}); pull O(|S'|)

key_findings.finding: Correctness: BMSSP returns the full set of vertices whose shortest path visits S, with all returned vertices complete. The top-level call with S = {s}, B = infinity finds all shortest paths.

limitations: Theoretical only. The text reports no implementation or experiments, so practical constants are unmeasured. The hidden constant C in the bounds is not quantified.

Computation model is the comparison-addition model only (real weights; each addition and comparison costs unit time). Integer-weight or word-RAM improvements are discussed as related work (Thorup 1999/2004), not as this paper's result.

Assumes constant in- and out-degree via a transformation (Sec. 2, p. 3). The transformation is stated to preserve shortest paths and yield O(m) vertices and edges. Assumes m >= n-1 and every vertex reachable from s (p. 3-4).
Assumes all path lengths are distinct (Assumption 2.1, p. 4). The paper argues a lexicographic tuple order makes this WLOG, using Pred[] and hop count alpha stored per bd[v] (p. 4).

Bound is O(m log^(2/3) n), which is superlinear on sparse graphs; the paper does not claim linear time. The result is for distances and does not produce the full distance ordering. The paper cites HHR+24 that Dijkstra is optimal if ordering is required (p. 1).
Partial executions of BMSSP are noted as more complex to analyze, and the paper introduces batch-prepend and FindPivots to handle them (Sec. 3.1, p. 5; Lemma 3.3, p. 7).

references_of_note: Dij59: Dijkstra (1959), the baseline O(m + n log n) SSSP algorithm.
Bel58: Bellman (1958), the k-round relaxation idea that FindPivots builds on.
GT88 / CKT+16 / DLWX18: Gabow-Tarjan (1988), Chechik et al. (2016), and Duan-Lyu-Wu-Xie (2018), the recursive partitioning and bottleneck-path methods the algorithm adapts.
DMSY23: Duan, Mao, Shu, Yin (FOCS 2023), randomized O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) SSSP for undirected graphs; this paper's direct predecessor.
HHR+24: Haeupler, Hladik, Rozhon, Tarjan, Tetek (FOCS 2024), Dijkstra optimal when vertex ordering is required.
Fre83: Frederickson (1983), the constant-degree graph transformation used in Sec. 2.
PR05: Pettie-Ramachandran (2005), the undirected hierarchy-based SSSP bound O(m alpha(m,n) + min{n log n, n log log r}).
Tho04: Thorup (2004), directed integer-weight SSSP in O(m + n log log min{n, C}).
None of the references concern lobbying, networks as social objects, elections, persuasion, turnout, legislators, or text measurement.

rel.summary_md:
Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu and Yin (arXiv 2504.17033v2, 2025; Paul's bib lists it as STOC 2025) give a deterministic single-source shortest-path algorithm for **directed** graphs with real non-negative weights that runs in O(m log^(2/3) n) in the comparison-addition model. It is the first to beat Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) on sparse graphs. The method combines Dijkstra with Bellman-Ford through a recursive bounded multi-source routine (BMSSP). FindPivots shrinks the frontier to at most |U|/k pivots, and a block-list structure sorts only partially, with k = log^(1/3) n and t = log^(2/3) n. The result covers distances only, with no full distance ordering. It is purely theoretical: there is no implementation, and the constant C is never given.

For Paul's systems this is a speed result with very little to transfer. Every route engine as built is either tiny (533 members, an O(N^2) array scan in the dashboard), a point-to-sink query that stops early (staffer closeness routes, bidirectional, plus Yen alternatives), or an integer-weight search (overlap routes). The paper's bound covers full single-source distances on sparse graphs with real weights, so none of these uses fits its model. The one real link is Assumption 2.1: the paper breaks ties by lexicographic order on (length, hop count, predecessor), which matches the staffer router's (cost, steps) tie rule. On latency, the staffer-network lane found the bottleneck was memory (pair_cache), not the heap's log n. ALT landmarks remain the deferred lever, and this paper does not replace them. While checking the dashboard's 'provably optimal' chain, I found a possible problem with edge direction (see flags). It is UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: O(m log^(2/3) n) beats Dijkstra only for single-source distances to ALL vertices, on sparse directed graphs (m = O(n) after a constant-degree transform), in the comparison-addition model. It returns distances without a full ordering. Dijkstra stays optimal when the ordering is required (HHR+24). The hidden constant C is not quantified and nothing is implemented.
bearings.paper_location: Theorem 1.1, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 1 (HHR+24); Sec. 2-3.1, pp. 3-4; Lemma 3.12, p. 14
bearings.system_side: The default office route is a point-to-sink search. It is bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 that stops once the frontier lower bounds pass the best meeting point. A second pass computes in exact integers, by scaling dyadic floats, and Yen's loopless alternatives need repeated shortest-path calls. On 2026-10-02 the latency cause was diagnosed as memory: pair_cache grew the sidecar from 7.0 to 17.5 GB. It was not heap cost. ALT landmarks are deferred.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The bound carries over only if the system ever needs full single-source distance fields over the ~4.66M-pair staffer graph, for example one origin to every office. Even then, the theoretical gain at n ~ 10^6-10^7 is about log n / log^(2/3) n, roughly 2.5-3x before an unknown constant. It does not carry over to early-stopping point-to-point queries, bidirectional search, Yen alternatives, or exact-tie passes, and it does not touch the measured memory bottleneck. Treat it as no recommendation to change the router.

bearings.paper_claim: Assumption 2.1 makes all path lengths distinct without loss of generality by comparing lexicographic tuples (length, hop count alpha, predecessor sequence), stored per bd[v] with Pred[].
bearings.system_side: Routes are keyed by (cost, steps). Costs within 1e-12 relative count as ties, and then fewest steps wins, then least exact cost, then the smallest node ids read from the sink end (Paul's 2026-10-03 tie ruling, D-082).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The (length, hops, then node id) order is the standard tie-breaker in algorithm theory, so it is not ad hoc, and any future algorithm that assumes distinct path lengths can keep it. The paper's comparisons are exact. The system's 1e-12 relative tie band is a separate tolerance that the paper does not cover.

bearings.paper_claim: The result holds in the comparison-addition model for real weights. Faster integer-weight bounds come from a different line of work, which the paper cites as related work: Thorup 2004 gives O(m + n log log min{n, C}) for directed integer weights in word RAM.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 1, pp. 1-3 (related work, Tho04; 'C is the maximum edge weight', highlighted by Paul, p. 3)
bearings.system_side: Overlap-route edge distances are integers, ceil(1e6 x 128 / strength), with a minimum of 1. The search is bidirectional Dijkstra on integer (cost, steps) keys.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Because the weights are integers, the relevant asymptotic line is the integer/word-RAM literature (Thorup), not this paper. Its comparison-addition guarantee still holds but is not the tightest bound. This matters only if overlap-route latency becomes heap-bound, which has not been shown.

bearings.paper_claim: Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) is beaten only asymptotically on sparse graphs, and the paper's analysis assumes a directed graph with non-negative weights where every vertex is reachable from s.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract and Theorem 1.1, p. 1; Sec. 2, pp. 3-4
bearings.system_side: The most-reliable recruitment chain uses distToTarget, a max-product Dijkstra that scans an array (no heap) over N = 533 members, O(N^2). A greedy trace then follows PE[cur][v] x dT[v]. PE is directed: the receiver's EMU[v], source_shock and target_resistance make PE[u][v] differ from PE[v][u].
bearings.transfer_conditions: At n = 533 the asymptotic gain is irrelevant: the O(N^2) scan is already instant in the browser. The paper adds nothing to the reliability semantics (-log p) or to the unestimated ASKM ask-lift. It is relevant only as a reminder that SSSP on a directed graph must relax edges in the direction of the query. See the flag on the direction of distToTarget.

gaps_exposed: No route engine has a heuristic or landmark speed-up: heuristic 0 everywhere (staffer_routing.py:381), and ALT is deferred. If latency matters, the paper's asymptotic SSSP gain is a weaker lever than goal-directed search or preprocessing such as ALT or contraction hierarchies, which the paper does not cover.

No measurement isolates how much staffer-route time is heap/priority-queue cost versus neighbor-evidence construction (pair_cache). Without that split, no faster-SSSP algorithm can be judged worthwhile.

The dashboard's most-reliable chain has no test against a reference shortest-path on the directed PE matrix, such as a reverse-graph Dijkstra oracle like the one staffer_closeness_routes keeps in _search_reference.
flags: UNVERIFIED (single-path agent reading, DE-062): distToTarget (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:734) seeds d[target] = 1 and relaxes d[v] = d[u] x PE[u][v]. On a directed PE that computes reliability FROM the target outward, but tracePath (:740) multiplies a forward edge PE[cur][v] by dT[v] as if dT were reliability TO the target. Edges are asymmetric here (EMU[v] at :586; source_shock/target_resistance at :595-597), so the 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL' comment (:735-737) holds only if PE is symmetric. The same class of reversed index was fixed at :633 on 2026-09-30. A second path should reproduce this before anyone acts. This finding does not come from the paper.

Wording: the dashboard code comment calls chain reliability 'the exact, maximal probability' and 'mathematical certainty' (:735-737). The UI tooltip (:1119, :1155) correctly says it is a scenario output, not an empirical probability. The comment should not be quoted as a claim about access or introduction probability (D-025 spirit).

Venue: the PDF read is arXiv v2 with no venue. Paul's bib gives STOC 2025, pp. 36-44, doi 10.1145/3717823.3718179. That is plausible but cannot be verified from the file, so cite the arXiv version unless the STOC version is checked.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 (LDA) or reciprocity rules: the paper takes no position on edge construction or weighting.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's two bibliography entries for this paper carry citations only, with no takeaways. His 26 highlights mark the headline claim, the Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford contrast, the frontier-shrinking idea and the comparison-addition model, so he read it as algorithm background. His stated path-finding gaps are not addressed here: he wants to turn lobbying and bipartite data into a routable graph and to use A* heuristics that cope with unstable information. This paper speeds up exact SSSP. It says nothing about graph construction, heuristics, dynamic replanning or probabilistic reliability. His notes are not stale, but the system has since moved on. The 2026-10-02 staffer-latency lane showed the routers are bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0, that the bottleneck was memory rather than sorting, and that ALT is deferred. A theoretical sorting-barrier result therefore has no current place in the build. Citing Duan under member-recruitment-path is accurate only as background.

related.why: It supplies the most-reliable-path (max-product, -log p) semantics that the dashboard recruitment chain implements. Duan only bounds the cost of the underlying shortest-path computation once the weights are non-negative logs.

It covers the heuristic and A* family that Paul names as his path-finding gap. Duan is the exact, heuristic-free line, and the two speed up different things: worst-case SSSP versus goal-directed search.

MOPBD* (multi-objective D* Lite) is the concept cited for the Pareto cosponsor route finder and for Paul's incremental-replanning layer. Duan's static single-objective SSSP does not cover dynamic or multi-objective cases.

It applies shortest-path algorithms to social-network tie strength, which is the modelling side (strongest path) that Duan's purely algorithmic result leaves out. Paul lists both under member-recruitment-path.
